strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP/speech question: whether Mamba can provide useful HuBERT-style representations while improving causal and long-context processing efficiency.

The experimental scope is broader than a single downstream task, covering causal and bidirectional models, two model scales, ASR fine-tuning, four SUPERB tasks, phone purity, representation analysis, and alternative bidirectional Mamba designs.

Several comparisons are reasonably controlled through matched pretraining procedures and approximately matched parameter counts. The paper also reports unfavorable results—especially the weak base-size bidirectional model—rather than presenting Mamba as uniformly superior.

The causal results are promising: base Mamba improves PR and causal-ASR WER over the causal Transformer despite having fewer parameters. Processing complete TED talks also yields a substantial WER improvement over utterance-level ExtBiMamba.
weaknesses: The manuscript is not adequately reproducible. It omits essential details including the SSL pretraining corpus, model dimensions and Mamba configuration, masking and optimization settings, target-clustering procedure, downstream splits and heads, ASR decoding setup, document construction, CCA datasets and estimation procedure, random seeds, and code/model availability. The brief statement that training follows HuBERT is insufficient because the procedure is materially modified.

Figure 1 appears internally incorrect or mislabeled. The reported “RTF” values are roughly 400–1800, the vertical axis is inverted, and the numerical values decrease as sequence length grows, while the text says RTF increases and that Mamba has lower values. Measurement conditions such as precision, batch size, caching, warm-up, and whether training or inference is measured are also absent. Consequently, the central empirical efficiency claim cannot presently be verified from the figure.

Calling the experiment “streaming ASR” is insufficiently justified. The paper describes causal attention but does not establish that the convolutional frontend and all other components avoid future context, nor does it report chunking, algorithmic latency, lookahead, state caching, or online decoding. A causal full-sequence evaluation is not by itself a streaming evaluation.

The long-context evidence does not isolate the benefit of the architecture. ExtBiMamba with document context is compared against a Transformer that is simply declared OOM on one 48-GB GPU; there are no memory-efficient or chunked-attention baselines, matched-memory comparisons, or a Transformer receiving comparable cross-utterance context. Thus the result demonstrates feasibility under one implementation more clearly than architectural superiority.

Most results appear to come from one training run, with no variance or robustness analysis. The paired t-test is underspecified—sample size, unit of analysis, test assumptions, and correction choices are absent—and paired bootstrap testing would be more standard for WER. Small SUPERB differences therefore should not support firm rankings.

The representation claims exceed the evidence. Higher phone purity only establishes stronger alignment under a particular clustering evaluation; no spoken-language-model experiment shows that the units are actually beneficial. Likewise, CCA against pretrained speaker or emotion embeddings does not directly establish better disentanglement or feature quality, and the paper omits controls for dimensionality, regularization, estimation bias, and significance.

The baseline coverage is too limited for the broad practical claims. Comparisons are largely confined to Transformers trained under the authors’ reduced-compute recipe, without established pretrained HuBERT results, efficient-attention or Conformer alternatives, recent streaming systems, or strong long-context baselines. This makes it difficult to separate Mamba's merits from implementation and training-budget effects.

The study contains potentially valuable exploratory evidence, but the contradictory efficiency plot, ambiguity of the streaming setup, limited statistical support, and substantial reproducibility omissions prevent a sound Findings recommendation in its current form. These issues appear addressable through corrected reporting, complete experimental specifications, stronger controls, and repeated runs, making resubmission next cycle plausible.

strengths: The paper studies an important and clearly relevant problem: replacing quadratic-attention HuBERT encoders with linear-time Mamba variants for causal, long-context, and general-purpose speech representation learning.

The empirical scope is broader than a single downstream task, covering computational scaling, long-context and causal ASR, representation analyses, four SUPERB tasks, two model sizes, and alternative bidirectional Mamba designs.

Training Transformer and Mamba baselines from scratch under the same reduced HuBERT training regime is a useful attempt at controlled comparison. Several comparisons also approximately match parameter counts.

The efficiency results and Transformer out-of-memory behavior provide plausible evidence that Mamba is attractive for very long inputs. The document-level ExtBiMamba result is promising, improving WER from 13.37 to 11.08.

The results are reported with useful nuance: Mamba is stronger in the causal setting and at the small bidirectional scale, but substantially worse than the Transformer at the base bidirectional scale.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not specify the pretraining corpus, data preprocessing, complete architecture configurations, optimizer and learning-rate schedule, hardware/training duration, downstream hyperparameters, decoding procedure, or random seeds. No code, models, or release commitment is stated.

Most accuracy results appear to come from single runs, with no uncertainty or robustness analysis. Several claimed advantages are small enough that seed variance could change the conclusions. The sole paired t-test does not identify the sampling unit, sample size, assumptions, or correction procedure.

The long-context ASR evidence is too limited for the central claim. It uses one dataset and one Mamba configuration, while the Transformer comparison is reported only as OOM. There are no memory-matched, chunked, sparse/local-attention, or other efficient long-context baselines, so the experiment establishes feasibility on the authors' setup rather than superior long-context ASR methodology.

The paper calls the causal ASR result “streaming ASR,” but does not describe incremental inference, state caching, chunking, emission latency, lookahead, or streaming decoding. Causality alone is insufficient to demonstrate a practical streaming system.

The causal ASR comparison is not capacity-matched: the 78.2M Mamba is compared with a 94.7M Transformer, while the available 94.7M Mamba+MLP variant is omitted. This prevents separating architectural effects from capacity or optimization differences.

Efficiency reporting is unclear and potentially misleading. Figure 1's RTF axis uses values in the hundreds to thousands and is visually inverted, without an explained scale or units. Peak memory is not reported, MAC methodology is unspecified, and timing only one GPU with ten runs but no variance, warm-up, precision, or implementation details does not support a rigorous systems comparison.

The representation claims overreach the evidence. Higher phone purity is not consistently reflected in phoneme recognition, and “beneficial for spoken language modeling” is asserted without evaluating a spoken language model. CCA against pretrained speaker/emotion embedding proxies does not by itself show that attributes are captured “more distinctly,” especially without procedural details, statistical tests, or controls for representation dimensionality.

The purportedly comprehensive general-purpose evaluation uses only four SUPERB tasks. The aggregate SUPERB score formula is not defined, per-task probing configurations are missing, and the mixed results—especially the large bidirectional model losing on every task—substantially limit the generality and scalability claims.

The document-level experiment lacks essential dataset construction details: the number and duration distribution of retained talks, how transcripts and CTC targets are aligned, train/dev/test handling, batching, decoding, and whether utterance- and document-level scores use exactly comparable audio and scoring conventions.

Overall, the central direction is plausible and potentially useful, but major experimental documentation, controlled baselines, repeated trials, and claim calibration are needed before the work meets the soundness and reproducibility threshold for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant question for speech representation learning and evaluates Mamba-based HuBERT models across complementary settings: computational efficiency, long-context and causal ASR, representation analysis, and SUPERB probing.

The controlled comparisons with Transformer-based HuBERT models trained under the same reduced-compute regimen provide useful evidence. Results consistently support Mamba's expected long-sequence efficiency, and the causal models improve phoneme recognition and overall SUPERB score while using comparable or fewer parameters.

The long-context TEDLIUM3 experiment is practically interesting: document-level ExtBiMamba improves WER from 13.37% to 11.08%, while the tested Transformer cannot fit in memory. The paper also reports a paired significance test for this comparison.

The results are presented clearly, including negative and scale-dependent findings: bidirectional Mamba substantially underperforms the Transformer at base scale, and the preferred bidirectional design changes with model size. This restraint strengthens the empirical contribution.
The topic is clearly relevant to computational linguistics, particularly efficient speech SSL, streaming recognition, and discrete speech-unit extraction.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript. It does not clearly identify the SSL pretraining corpus, data preparation, full model configurations, optimizer and learning-rate settings, hardware/training time, downstream training and decoding details, random seeds, or code availability. Several analysis datasets and sampling procedures are also unspecified.

The evidence for robustness is limited. Most downstream results appear to be single runs without uncertainty or significance testing, despite modest differences in several SUPERB comparisons. The long-context t-test does not state the number and definition of paired observations or verify the assumptions behind the test.

The claim of superior streaming ASR is stronger than the evidence. The experiment establishes causal ASR performance, but does not evaluate an actual streaming setup, chunking policy, algorithmic latency, lookahead, state caching, or a latency-accuracy tradeoff.

The long-context comparison is informative but incomplete: it uses one dataset, compares against a Transformer implementation that runs out of memory rather than memory-efficient or chunked attention baselines, and does not fully control whether gains arise from context, segmentation, or decoding differences. Qualitative claims about repeated rare words lack systematic measurements or examples.

The efficiency evaluation needs clearer definitions and controls. The plotted RTF magnitudes are difficult to interpret as conventional real-time factors, measurement details such as batch size and precision are absent, and some comparisons involve different parameter counts. Peak memory and streaming inference with recurrent-state caching are not reported.

The representation claims are somewhat overstated. Higher phone purity or CCA similarity does not by itself establish higher-quality or more distinctly encoded representations. K-means fitting details, CCA dimensionality and regularization, sample sizes, and uncertainty are omitted; moreover, the phone-purity and downstream PR results do not consistently agree.

Overall, the study is promising and close to a Findings contribution, but missing experimental specification and insufficient validation of the streaming, long-context, and representation-analysis claims prevent a clear sound-and-reproducible recommendation in its current form. These concerns appear addressable in a revision rather than requiring fundamental reconstruction.

strengths: The paper studies a relevant problem: replacing Transformer blocks in speech self-supervised models with linear-time Mamba variants, with attention to causal, long-context, and bidirectional settings.

The empirical scope is broader than a single downstream task. It includes ASR fine-tuning, efficiency measurements, phone-purity and CCA analyses, four-task probing, and a full 10-task SUPERB evaluation for representative models.

Training Transformer baselines from scratch under the same constrained HuBERT recipe improves comparability, and several comparisons approximately control model size. The causal results are reasonably consistent: Mamba variants improve phoneme recognition and the aggregate SUPERB score, including in the full benchmark.

The long-sequence experiments demonstrate a credible practical efficiency advantage under the tested implementation and hardware: Mamba processes sequences for which the standard attention implementation runs out of memory.

The paper reports informative negative results rather than presenting Mamba as uniformly superior. In particular, base-size bidirectional Mamba substantially underperforms the Transformer, and the architecture and scale ablations reveal useful instability and scalability limitations.
The presentation is generally clear, and the tables and figures make the principal empirical trends easy to follow.
weaknesses: The evidence does not cleanly support several central claims. The long-document ASR comparison has no runnable Transformer result and tests no memory-efficient attention, chunked, local-attention, or comparable long-context baseline. OOM on one conventional implementation establishes an engineering advantage under that setup, but not general superiority for long-context ASR.

The improvement from 13.37 to 11.08 WER does not isolate the value of meaningful document context. Document-level and utterance-level training alter segmentation and batching, and there are no controls using shuffled or unrelated context. The paired t-test is insufficiently documented: the unit of analysis, sample count, assumptions, and effect uncertainty are absent.

The paper describes the causal experiment as streaming ASR, but does not evaluate incremental state-cached inference, chunk processing, latency, memory over a stream, or endpoint behavior. A causal full-sequence WER result alone does not substantiate the claimed streaming advantage.

Representation analyses are seriously underspecified. The datasets, sample sizes, train/test separation, clustering protocol, phone alignment source, CCA dimensionality and regularization, and uncertainty estimates are not reported. CCA similarity to another pretrained speaker or emotion embedding does not by itself show that an attribute is represented “more distinctly” and may instead reflect retained nuisance information.

The claim that Mamba produces higher-quality quantized representations beneficial to spoken language models is stronger than the evidence. Phone purity is only a proxy, no spoken-language-model downstream experiment is conducted, and the paper itself observes that higher purity does not consistently translate into better phoneme probing.

All pretrained models are based on a single run, with no seeds, error bars, or variability estimates. This is consequential for small differences and especially for conclusions about architecture-by-scale effects when ExtBiMamba is reported to train unstably.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the submitted manuscript. The promised codebase link is blank, while key architecture and fine-tuning details are missing, including the appended 12-layer convolutional encoder specification, batching and document construction, decoding setup, efficiency-measurement procedure, precision and kernel configuration, and analysis data pipelines.

The aggregate four-task score is inconsistently documented: the experiments use intent classification, whereas Appendix C says the task set includes slot filling. Reliance on an aggregate normalized against external SOTA values also needs clearer reporting of the exact constants and implementation.

The contribution is primarily a systematic architecture substitution and evaluation. Closely related work already studies Mamba-based speech SSL and long-context or streaming speech models, and the paper does not experimentally compare against those systems. This limits novelty and makes the “first comprehensive exploration” claim difficult to assess.

Overall, the study contains promising and plausibly sound empirical observations, but the confounded long-context result, unsupported streaming and representation claims, missing methodological detail, and lack of replication prevent a clear Findings recommendation in its current form. These concerns appear addressable with narrower claims, complete specifications and code, controlled long-context baselines, and uncertainty reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP/speech question and provides a reasonably broad empirical study spanning causal and bidirectional HuBERT pretraining, ASR fine-tuning, representation analyses, and SUPERB evaluation. Review based on the complete manuscript: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/fa4ff843834d4e65a694da714baa1fab/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The causal experiments show a consistent and practically interesting pattern: Mamba variants outperform a causally pretrained Transformer on phoneme recognition, speaker identification, aggregate SUPERB scores, and causal ASR, sometimes with fewer parameters.

The efficiency measurements cover inputs from 5 to 320 seconds and support the expected practical advantage of linear-time sequence modeling. The document-level TEDLIUM3 result is a useful demonstration that the Mamba model can process inputs that exhaust the memory of the tested full-attention baseline.

Including parameter-matched variants, small and base model sizes, multiple bidirectional Mamba designs, several clustering granularities, and a full ten-task SUPERB evaluation strengthens the empirical coverage.

The paper reports important negative findings rather than presenting Mamba as uniformly superior: base-size bidirectional Mamba substantially underperforms the Transformer, and the authors document training instability.
weaknesses: The claimed streaming-ASR contribution is not adequately demonstrated. The experiment reports offline WER for a causal encoder, but evaluates neither stateful chunk-by-chunk inference nor latency, emission delay, memory growth, endpointing, or streaming RTF. Causality alone does not establish a competitive streaming system, so the abstract and contributions overstate the evidence.

The long-context experiment lacks decisive controls. It compares document-level Mamba against utterance-level Mamba while the Transformer simply receives an OOM result. This conflates access to context with changes in segmentation, batching, optimization, and evaluation. There is no memory-efficient, chunked, local-attention, or hierarchical Transformer baseline, nor a context-length ablation showing where the WER gain arises.

The statistical analysis is insufficient. All pretrained models use a single run, despite differences that are often small. The paired t-test for document- versus utterance-level WER does not define its observational units and is not clearly appropriate for corpus-level ASR errors; confidence intervals or paired bootstrap/MAPSSWE-style tests are absent. No significance or variance analysis is supplied for SUPERB, phone purity, or CCA.

Several representation claims exceed what the analyses establish. Higher cluster phone purity does not by itself demonstrate better speech units for spoken-language modeling, which is never evaluated. Likewise, greater CCA correlation with embeddings from a separate speaker model is not sufficient evidence that speaker information is represented more distinctly; dataset size, train/test separation, dimensionality control, regularization, and uncertainty for CCA are unspecified, leaving substantial risk of overfitting or confounding.

Architectural conclusions are confounded by optimization choices. Base bidirectional Mamba uses a peak learning rate of 5e-5 while other configurations use 5e-4, and the paper reports persistent mixed-precision loss-scale instability. Consequently, the claimed bidirectional scaling limitation may reflect an under-tuned or unstable training recipe rather than an inherent architectural property.

Efficiency reporting is incomplete and occasionally imprecise. The paper calls MACs per second “computational cost” and describes it as nearly constant with sequence length, although total MACs still grow linearly. It does not fully specify precision, batch size, kernels, compilation, attention implementation, memory measurements, warm-up protocol, or causal-state caching. The OOM comparison therefore demonstrates behavior of the tested implementations, not a general practical boundary between the architectures.

Reproducibility falls below the Findings threshold. The abstract's code link is blank, and essential details are missing for architecture dimensions, fine-tuning schedules, decoding and language-model use, document construction and alignment, downstream heads, k-means sampling and seeds, CCA data and preprocessing, and evaluation sample counts. References to “default” HuBERT or SUPERB settings do not resolve configuration choices that materially affect the results.

The contribution is primarily a benchmarking exploration built from existing HuBERT, Mamba, and bidirectional-Mamba components, with substantial conceptual overlap with prior work on Mamba-based speech SSL. Breadth is useful, but the paper does not articulate sharply enough what new scientific conclusion is established beyond known linear-scaling behavior and task-dependent empirical comparisons. Important additional experiments and reporting are needed before the central claims are sound and reproducible, making resubmission next cycle more appropriate than Findings acceptance.

strengths: The paper provides a useful and unusually broad empirical study of Mamba-based HuBERT models, covering causal and bidirectional variants, computational scaling, ASR fine-tuning, representation analysis, and both reduced and full SUPERB evaluations.

The central causal-setting result is supported consistently across several measurements: Mamba is more efficient on long sequences and generally improves phonetic/content and speaker-related tasks over a causally pretrained Transformer, sometimes with fewer parameters.

The comparisons are reasonably controlled: Mamba and Transformer baselines use the same 960-hour data and training pipeline, parameter-matched variants are included, and the paper openly reports unfavorable results, particularly the substantial base-scale bidirectional gap.

The long-document ASR experiment demonstrates a practically relevant capability: ExtBiMamba can process full TEDLIUM3 talks and improves from 13.37 to 11.08 WER, whereas the tested Transformer configuration runs out of memory.

The analysis of multiple bidirectional designs and training-loss scaling is informative. The scale-dependent reversal between ExtBiMamba and InnBiMamba provides useful guidance and avoids presenting Mamba as uniformly superior.
The paper is relevant to speech and NLP, clearly organized, and appropriately acknowledges limited training scale, single-run results, and Mamba's weaker bidirectional performance.
weaknesses: The efficiency evidence is insufficiently specified and appears internally confusing. Figure 1 reports purported real-time factors in the hundreds or thousands, uses an unusual axis presentation, and does not define timing details such as precision, batching, warm-up, compilation, recurrent-state caching, or whether optimized attention kernels were used. The causal Transformer becoming OOM much earlier than the bidirectional Transformer suggests an implementation-specific mask overhead rather than an inherent architectural limitation.

The paper equates causal evaluation with streaming ASR but does not report an actual stateful/chunked streaming experiment, latency, memory over an indefinitely growing stream, or endpointing behavior. Thus the evidence supports causal ASR, not the stronger real-time or streaming deployment claim.

All pretrained models are represented by a single run. No uncertainty is reported for ASR or SUPERB results, so modest differences such as 15.77 versus 16.66 WER and several small probing gains cannot confidently be separated from training or fine-tuning variance. The paired t-test for long-context ASR also lacks the sampling unit, sample count, effect distribution, and test assumptions.

The representation analyses omit essential reproducibility details: the evaluation datasets and sample sizes are not clearly identified, and the CCA fitting protocol, dimensionality, regularization, and held-out evaluation procedure are unspecified. Higher CCA with a pretrained speaker embedding also does not by itself establish that speaker factors are represented more distinctly.

Several conclusions overreach the evidence. Phone purity is only a proxy for quantized-unit quality, and no spoken-language-model experiment establishes that the units are beneficial in that application. Likewise, the long-context gain is shown for one model and dataset without controlled context-length ablations or a memory-efficient Transformer baseline.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated emphasis on it: the code link is blank in the manuscript, downstream fine-tuning and decoding configurations are mostly delegated to prior defaults, long-document batching and construction are underspecified, and hardware for the fine-tuning OOM comparison is unclear. Appendix C also inconsistently names slot filling although the four-task score in the main experiments uses intent classification.

The contribution is chiefly an empirical exploration rather than a new modeling or training method. Together with the limited datasets, missing uncertainty, and incomplete efficiency controls, this supports a solid Findings contribution but not a confident main-conference recommendation.
